newsitem.title: INDIA: India prime rate cuts seen limited by low spreads.
newsitem.headline: India prime rate cuts seen limited by low spreads.

text.p: Indian banks are likely to reduce prime lending rates following a central bank cut in its bank rate but they will be constrained by profitability considerations, analysts said on Thursday.
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) on Wednesday announced a cut in bank rate to 10 percent per annum from 11 percent.
It also announced a one percentage point cut in deposit rates, saying banks can now offer a maximum of eight percent per annum on deposits with maturities of 30 days to one year.
Bankers said they will consider cuts in prime rates over the coming days but analysts cautioned that major reductions in lending rates will hit bank bottomlines.
"We have to see how banks react," said Sandeep Nanda, research head at NatWest Markets. "It all depends how much banks cut prime lending rates and deposit rates."
Nanda said the impact of a 50 basis point cut in prime lending rates could be neutralised if deposit rates also came down by 100 basis points.
"But a steeper fall in lending rates will hit banks hard," he said. "We think a one percentage point cut in prime rates could result in bank profits dropping by five percent."
Other analysts agreed, saying spreads were already under pressure from lending rate cuts in the last year.
Banks cut prime rates by 150-200 basis points last year after borrowers complained of the high cost of borrowings and the RBI inititiated measures to reduce interest rates.
"Spreads are already under pressure," said S.R. Krishnan, banking analyst at Peregrine Capital India Ltd. "We expect margins to drop further this year."
"Further there is a basic question whether lower interest rates will boost credit offtake at all," Krishnan said.

The series of interest rate reductions over the past year have had little impact on loan disbursals, as economic growth slowed and corporates were less confident about investing. And consequent excess liquidity continues to plague banks.
The impact of last year's cuts on profitability were yet to be felt, warned another analyst.

"Last year's revision in rates will be probably be felt this year...if banks have to take another hit now, we could see bottomlines taking a beating," said Dick H. Mody, banking analyst at ICICI Securities and Finance Company.
"I think it will be best for them if banks do not cut prime lending rates," Mody said.
"Whenever there is a fall in interest rates, banks get hit as the reduced interest rates apply to all advances but the revised deposit rates apply only to fresh deposits," he said.
Mody felt banks depending on long-term funds could be hit harder.
"Most of the new private sector banks depend more on short-term deposits," he said. "They will be benefited as their cost of funds will come down."
The one percentage point cut announced by the RBI applies to deposits with maturities of 30 days up to one year. Rates for deposits above one year are unregulated.
NatWest's Nanda said bank revenue streams will also be hit by the reduction in export credit interest rates as loans to exporters comprised 10-12 percent of bank advances.
The RBI had announced a one percentage point cut in interest rates on post-shipment rupee export credit along with the other measures on Wednesday.
